claim: Of 163 million registered online freelancer profiles worldwide, only 14 million (8.6 percent) have ever obtained work through the platform and only 3.3 million (2.0 percent) have completed at least 10 projects or earned at least US$1,000.
stance_target: The position that platform-mediated earning has a funnel in which roughly 98 percent of registrants never reach any meaningful cumulative income
scope_conditions: Global; online FREELANCING platforms (Upwork, Freelancer, Amazon Mechanical Turk and similar), NOT content-creation platforms; 2020 data published 2021 in Open Research Europe, peer-reviewed, DOI 10.12688/openreseurope.13639.4; 140 million profiles directly observed plus 23 million model-predicted
quoted_support: Our headline estimate is that there are 163 million freelancer profiles registered on online labour platforms globally. Approximately 14 million of them have obtained work through the platform at least once, and 3.3 million have completed at least 10 projects or earned at least $1000.

claim: The famous 8.6 percent active-worker figure rests on directly observed activity data from only 7 platforms, and the significantly-worked figure on only 6, so the authors refused to compute a confidence interval and published an observed range of 2.0 to 36.8 percent instead.
stance_target: The treatment of the 8.6 percent active-share statistic as a precise measurement, as it is used in ILO and World Bank secondary citations that omit the sample size
scope_conditions: Global; online freelancing platforms; 2020 data; error bands are minimum and maximum observed values in the sample, not statistical confidence intervals
quoted_support: We note, that only a handful of platforms reveal this information publicly, the sample sizes for these estimates remain very small. Thus, instead of calculating a formal confidence interval for these estimates, we use the minimum and maximum values of the samples as our error band estimate in sensitivity analyses.

claim: The World Bank's 37 percent mean active-worker share does not contradict Kassi et al.'s 8.6 percent so much as sit at the extreme top of their observed range, since 36.8 percent was the highest single-platform ever-worked share in their 7-platform sample.
stance_target: The apparent fourfold contradiction between World Bank and Oxford Internet Institute estimates of platform activity rates
scope_conditions: Global; comparison between Kassi et al. (2021) observed platform data and the World Bank (2023) traffic-proxy model over 503 platforms; both concern online gig platforms, not content platforms; the reconciliation is an inference from the published error bands, not a statement either source makes
quoted_support: for rows (c), and (d) the error bands are calculated as minimum and maximum values in the data

claim: Registered platform accounts grew from 50 million in 2015 to 163 million in 2020 while the active share fell from 10 percent to 8.6 percent, meaning the platform economy added registrations roughly three times faster than it added people who actually earn.
stance_target: The position that growth in the number of people attempting platform-based income vastly outpaces growth in the number who succeed, so the success rate declines as entry grows
scope_conditions: Global; comparison of Kuek et al. (2015) with Kassi et al. (2021); the authors note the two estimates use different methods and that applying Kuek's assumptions to their own data would have yielded 130 million rather than 163 million
quoted_support: These numbers suggest a substantial growth from 2015 in registered worker accounts, but much less growth in amount of work completed by workers.

claim: The authors interpret their own finding as evidence of oversupply, stating that platform work is a viable living for only a small minority of registrants.
stance_target: The position that the low active share reflects labour oversupply rather than casual or exploratory registration alone
scope_conditions: Global; online freelancing platforms; 2020 data; the authors' own reading of their headline result
quoted_support: the fact that only a small minority have completed any projects, let alone a substantial number of projects suggest that digital platform work is a viable way to make a living only to a small minority of registered workers.

claim: Headcounts of platform workers are inflated by multi-homing and deflated by account sharing: workers are registered on an average of 1.83 platforms while 21 percent report having worked under a shared or borrowed account.
stance_target: The reliability of registered-account counts as a proxy for the number of distinct people attempting platform income
scope_conditions: Global; multi-homing parameter derived from ILO (2021) and Wood et al. (2019a) surveys of active freelancers; the authors concede it is a non-representative convenience sample; account-sharing derived from three yes/no survey items
quoted_support: Across the surveys, 48% of the respondents mentioned that they worked exclusively on a single platform. On average, the survey respondents were active on 1.83 platforms.
numbers: 7.7 million and 1.8 million after multi-homing adjustment
9.3 million and 2.2 million after multi-working adjustment
